Google Translate Banned Me for trying to Learn How to Say "tienes que volver". Tee_un_ess_Ka_Hol_vey

Tee ennis ka hol vere ...T'enis kahhol verre...

Something like that.

My Spanish is a little rusty, but "tiennes" means to possess something. Tiennes un lapiz or even hunger - tiennes hambre.

I'm not sure if it's the best word for the situation, maybe whatever the word for "need" is.

"tener que" translates to "have to (do something)"

It's fine here.

"Tienes que volver" while understandable, is very literal. I would try using something like: "Que regrese/regresen a su país pronto," or "Debes/Deben regresar a tu/su país." I would use either the former or latter after the / depending on whether I am talking to one person (former) or a group (latter). Volver/Regresar have greyish nuances to them... When used alone they imply "come back to where you are now," which you don't want. You want them to leave for someplace else, so you need to slap the preposition "a" in there to make it a transitive verb phrase with an object after it (their country, for example, Mexico. "Debes regresar a Mexico.")

"Tienes que" comes from the phrase "Tener que". While it is translated as " have to" I understand it as more of a construction used for general bitching; more indicative in nature than volitional. (EG. "Mierda, mañana, tengo que hacer un examen," "Tienes que volver a la iglesia despues de follarte a un malandro," "Los miembros de MS-13 tienen que ir a Taco Bell si están con hambre.") Having all of the immigrants go back is major event that you want to be over when it's over, so sentence constructions with Deber (must/should) seem like a better option to use to reflect the gravity the issue. Constructions with "Que" can be softer or harder than "Deber" ones, depending on tone and context.

Direct English to Spanish translations aren't so great. Spanish is a "snappy" language, English is more functional/blunt unless deliberately using constructions such as compound nouns for effect. I could be wrong somewhere because I am going by memory, but a spic goat can always just build on what I said with corrections.

Also, "Tienes que volver" would be pronounced "Tee-en-ess keh bol bare" or something like that. The "b" and long "a" are going to be a bit more soft in enunciation than in English.
